$comment: What the declaration means here is the API surface, not the datacentre. A
route that declares `edge` promises to use only what a V8 isolate offers —
`Request`, `Response`, `fetch`, `URL`, `crypto` — and the build refuses it if
anything in its module graph reaches for a Node built-in that an isolate does
not have. That is the property the whole edge story rests on: it is what
makes the route runnable on Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Edge, or Deno Deploy
Where the route physically runs is then the adapter's business, and it is
always safe for a Node host to answer an edge route — every API an edge route
may use exists in Node too, so the constraint is a subset rather than a
different set. The route manifest carries the declaration so an adapter that
can place work on an edge network has the information to do it; an adapter
that cannot simply serves the route from its function, correctly.

$declarationNote: Accepted values and what each resolves to in the route manifest. An
unrecognised value is refused rather than defaulted: the export exists
because the author meant somewhere specific, and reading `'Edge'` as Node
would move the route with nothing said.
$builtinNote: Node built-ins an edge route may not reach, by bare name or under the
`node:` prefix. The list is deliberately conservative: it names the modules
that need a filesystem, a process table, or a socket, and leaves out the ones
every edge runtime ships a polyfill for. A name absent from both lists is not
checked — a false refusal on a module that does work costs more than a
missing one, because the missing one still fails loudly at deploy time.
